WESTERN EUROPE vs SOUTHEAST ASIA – IS IT TIME TO LOOK EAST?

Having spent much of my career working across Southeast Asia, and nearly two decades in executive search, I've seen some significant changes in both markets. One thing that strikes me today is just how different their respective outlooks have become.

Much of Western Europe is stuck in a rather cautious environment. Germany is struggling with its industrial base, France has its economic and political challenges, and the UK recruitment market remains subdued.

Companies are holding back, scrutinising costs and taking considerably longer to make senior hiring decisions. There is no shortage of talented executives, but fewer opportunities for many of them to make their next career move.

Now compare that with what's happening in Southeast Asia.
Vietnam continues to attract manufacturing investment. Thailand remains an important regional business hub. Malaysia is seeing growing interest in technology and advanced manufacturing, while Indonesia offers enormous opportunities for businesses prepared to invest for the longer term.

Of course, Southeast Asia has its challenges. It isn't a perfect market, and doing business here requires patience, local knowledge and an understanding of very different business cultures.

But there is something that stands out: ambition and an appetite for growth.
Businesses are expanding, investment is coming in, and companies need experienced people who can turn those opportunities into commercial results.

That means demand for good leadership – Managing Directors, CEOs, CFOs, COOs, Country Managers and senior operational and technology executives.
There is another opportunity here that I think many European businesses and executives are overlooking.

European companies expanding their Asian operations need experienced regional leadership. And executives who have spent 20 or 30 years building businesses, managing international operations or leading major transformations in Europe could bring enormous value to Southeast Asian organisations.

Why restrict a career search to London, Frankfurt, Paris or Amsterdam when Bangkok, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta and Ho Chi Minh City are increasingly important business centres?

Equally, Southeast Asian companies should not automatically limit their executive searches to candidates already living in the region.

Sometimes the best person for the job is sitting on the other side of the world.
My own view is that Southeast Asia will offer some very interesting opportunities over the next decade, both for businesses and internationally experienced executives.

Western Europe has the experience and established corporate infrastructure. Southeast Asia has growth markets, investment and a real appetite to expand.
I know which direction I'd be looking in.

Perhaps it's time more European executives did the same.

The Next AI Infrastructure Race: Technology Is Not Enough — Ecosystem Leadership Matters

Elon Musk’s public expression of interest in hiring Jensen Huang has sparked an interesting conversation across the technology industry.

But beyond the headlines, I believe there is a much bigger question worth exploring:

What makes a leader truly valuable in the AI infrastructure era?

Jensen Huang’s contribution to NVIDIA goes far beyond GPU innovation.

Over the past three decades, NVIDIA has built an ecosystem connecting semiconductor technology, computing architecture, networking, software developers, server manufacturers, cloud providers and enterprise customers.

This is not simply a technology business. It is an integrated industrial ecosystem.

And this is where the significance of Musk’s interest becomes particularly interesting.

As AI infrastructure continues to scale, competitive advantages will increasingly depend on more than access to advanced chips or computing capacity.

They will depend on the ability to connect multiple critical resources:

• Technology: GPUs, AI servers, networking and computing platforms.

• Energy: Reliable power supply, energy storage and efficiency.

• Infrastructure: Data centers, land, cooling and connectivity.

• Capital: Long-term investment and financing capabilities.

• Ecosystem: Strategic partnerships, supply chains, enterprise customers and execution capabilities.

These elements do not operate independently. Their value comes from how effectively they are integrated.

For Southeast Asia, this presents both an opportunity and a challenge.

Markets such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia are increasingly important in the regional AI infrastructure landscape. However, sustainable growth will require more than building data center capacity.

It will require stronger coordination between investors, infrastructure developers, technology providers, energy partners and enterprise customers.

My takeaway:

The next phase of AI infrastructure competition may not be won by those who simply own the most advanced technology or the largest computing capacity.

It may be shaped by those who can bring the right resources, partners and capabilities together — and turn them into commercially viable, scalable ecosystems.

In the AI era, ecosystem leadership could become one of the most important competitive advantages.

Challenge for Every City in the World: Waste Management and Urgent Need of Clean Energy

Cities and industries around the world face a dual crisis: escalating municipal solid waste and urgent need also for reliable, clean energy. Traditional waste-to-energy systems often struggle with high-moisture municipal waste and generate heavy emissions.

At BioCom Indonesia, we are engineering closed-loop infrastructure to turn municipal waste management into a continuous, zero-waste clean hydrogen engine.

Here is how our 3-stage integrated system works:

1. Hydrothermal Carbonization (HTC)

Mixed wet and dry municipal waste enters an Inconel pressurized thermal reactor without requiring energy-intensive pre-drying. Under controlled heat and pressure, organic and carbon-rich waste converts rapidly into energy-dense hydrochar (C).

2. Hydrochar Gasification

The resulting hydrochar moves into a high-temperature gasification unit, converting solid carbon into clean syngas—primarily carbon monoxide (CO) andhydrogen (H₂).

3. Perpetual Steam-Iron Process (Fe / Fe₃O₄)

Using a porous bed of iron and magnetite pellets, steam reacts with iron (Fe) to release high-purity green hydrogen gas (H₂) while forming magnetite (Fe₃O₄). The CO produced in Stage 2 is looped back into the reactor to reduce Fe₃O₄ back into elemental Fe—allowing the hydrogen generation cycle to repeat perpetually in a closed material loop.

By combining modular waste carbonization with chemical-looping hydrogen production, we can achieve99.8% mass balance efficiency and75%+ embodied carbon reduction—transforming urban waste liabilities into scalable clean energy assets.

My latest piece in @ForbesME

Will the Next Inflation Shock Start on the Farm?

The next inflation shock may not begin at the petrol pump. It could emerge months later in the fields as farmers grapple with constrained fertilizer supplies, elevated diesel costs, and a strong El Niño just as planting and application decisions lock in.

Key points from the article:

- Energy markets react instantly; agriculture runs on a seasonal calendar. Higher input costs today show up as lower yields and tighter supplies later.
- Fertilizer is the quiet bottleneck: ~47% of traded sulfur (critical for phosphate) normally moves through the Strait of Hormuz. Sulfur prices spiked hard, major producers like Mosaic cut guidance, and farmers in key markets are expected to apply significantly less.
- Diesel is another squeeze, the Middle East and Russia normally account for half of global net diesel exports, and prices have roughly doubled since the conflict began.
- Biofuel mandates (e.g., Indonesia’s palm oil biodiesel) add competing demand for agricultural feedstocks.
- A very strong El Niño (>90% probability of a strong event) arrives while crops may be under-fertilized and less resilient.
- FAO Food Price Index already hit its highest since late 2022; cereals are up sharply year-on-year. The lagged effects could feed into protein costs, hit lower-income countries hardest, and complicate central-bank easing.

None of this makes a full-blown food crisis inevitable, markets adapt, but headline commodity prices alone are a poor guide. Watch fertilizer availability, sulfur and phosphate flows, diesel exports, planting decisions, and yield revisions.
